signs__ENDOCRINE__Hirsutism & Virilisati.back: Central obesity, purple striae, proximal myopathy, easy bruising, hypertension and hyperglycaemia; screen with a dexamethasone suppression test.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hirsutism & Virilisati.front: What is non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia and how is it detected?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hirsutism & Virilisati.back: A milder 21-hydroxylase deficiency causing hirsutism (often from puberty) that can mimic PCOS; detected by a raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
Anabolic/androgenic steroids, danazol, some progestogens and ciclosporin; the timing follows the drug and it is usually reversible on stopping.
Regular menstrual cycles, normal androgen levels and no virilisation, reflecting increased hair-follicle sensitivity to normal androgens; it is a diagnosis of exclusion.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hirsutism & Virilisati.front: Why is new hirsutism or virilisation after the menopause concerning?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hirsutism & Virilisati.back: It is abnormal and raises the possibility of an androgen-secreting tumour, so it warrants measurement of testosterone/DHEAS and imaging.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hirsutism & Virilisati.front: Which investigations image a suspected androgen-secreting tumour?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hirsutism & Virilisati.back: Pelvic (transvaginal) ultrasound for an ovarian source and adrenal CT for an adrenal source, guided by whether testosterone or DHEAS is elevated.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hirsutism & Virilisati.front: What is the first-line medical treatment for hirsutism in PCOS/idiopathic hirsutism?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hirsutism & Virilisati.back: A combined oral contraceptive, with an anti-androgen (e.g. cyproterone acetate or spironolactone) if needed — anti-androgens are teratogenic, so the co-prescribed contraceptive is essential — plus lifestyle/weight loss, eflornithine cream and cosmetic measures.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hirsutism & Virilisati.front: Which additional hormone should be checked when hirsutism occurs with galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hirsutism & Virilisati.back: Prolactin, as coexisting hyperprolactinaemia may contribute; TFTs are also checked.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.front: What is gynaecomastia and what underlies it?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.back: True glandular breast tissue in a male, resulting from an imbalance between oestrogen and androgen action (relative oestrogen excess).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.front: How is gynaecomastia distinguished from pseudogynaecomastia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.back: Gynaecomastia has a firm, rubbery, disc of glandular tissue concentric to the nipple; pseudogynaecomastia is soft fatty enlargement (in obesity) with no discrete disc.
The neonatal period, puberty (common, tender and self-limiting), and older age (falling testosterone).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.front: What is the commonest pathological cause of gynaecomastia in adults?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.back: Drugs — e.g. spironolactone, digoxin, cimetidine, anti-androgens, finasteride, cannabis, anabolic steroids, and some antipsychotics/antiretrovirals. A medication review is essential.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.front: Which features suggest male breast cancer rather than benign gynaecomastia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.back: A hard, eccentric (off-centre), fixed, usually unilateral lump with nipple retraction, bleeding or skin change and axillary lymphadenopathy; it needs imaging and biopsy.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.front: Why must the testes always be examined in gynaecomastia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.back: Because a testicular tumour (hCG- or oestrogen-secreting) can cause gynaecomastia, particularly with rapid onset; examine the testes and send hCG/AFP.
Chronic liver disease (reduced oestrogen clearance, plus alcohol), chronic kidney disease, hyperthyroidism and hyperprolactinaemia.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.front: What is Klinefelter's syndrome and how does it relate to gynaecomastia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.back: A form of primary hypogonadism (47,XXY) with tall stature, small firm testes and infertility; it causes gynaecomastia and is confirmed by karyotype.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.front: What investigations are appropriate for unexplained adult gynaecomastia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.back: LFTs, U&E, TFTs, testosterone, LH/FSH, oestradiol, prolactin and hCG/AFP; testicular ultrasound for a mass, and mammography/ultrasound with biopsy for a suspicious breast lump.
With reassurance and review, as it is common and usually resolves spontaneously within months to a couple of years.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.front: What are the treatment options for persistent or distressing gynaecomastia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.back: Treat/remove the underlying cause (stop culprit drugs, treat systemic disease), and consider tamoxifen or surgery for persistent, tender or cosmetically distressing cases.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.front: Which examination features point to a benign gynaecomastia rather than cancer?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Gynaecomastia.back: A tender, firm, concentric (central) disc of tissue behind the nipple, often bilateral, without fixation, nipple retraction or nodes.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.front: What is galactorrhoea and what does it signify?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.back: Milky nipple discharge unrelated to breast-feeding; it is a sign of hyperprolactinaemia. It is typically milky, bilateral and from multiple ducts.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.front: How do you distinguish galactorrhoea from pathological breast discharge?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.back: Galactorrhoea is milky, bilateral and multi-duct. Pathological breast discharge is unilateral, blood-stained and from a single duct, suggesting a duct papilloma or carcinoma, and requires breast imaging and referral.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.front: What must be excluded first in a woman of reproductive age with galactorrhoea?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.back: Pregnancy — a pregnancy test (beta-hCG) is mandatory before further work-up.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.front: What is the commonest secondary (drug) cause of hyperprolactinaemia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.back: Dopamine antagonists — antipsychotics, metoclopramide and domperidone; also opioids and some antidepressants. A medication review is essential.
Raised TRH stimulates prolactin release; correcting the hypothyroidism normalises the prolactin. Check TFTs in every case.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.front: What features suggest a macroprolactinoma rather than a microprolactinoma?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.back: A very high prolactin with mass-effect symptoms — headache, a bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal compression) and hypopituitarism; MRI defines the tumour.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.front: What is the 'hook effect' in prolactin assays?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.back: A very large prolactinoma can produce a falsely low prolactin reading due to assay saturation; if the picture fits, ask the laboratory to dilute the sample.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.front: What is macroprolactin and why does it matter?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.back: A biologically inactive, high-molecular-weight complex that can cause an apparently raised prolactin without symptoms; it should be excluded before treating.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.front: Which investigations are appropriate for galactorrhoea?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.back: Pregnancy test, serum prolactin (fasting, rested, repeated, with a macroprolactin screen), TFTs and U&E; pituitary MRI if the prolactin is high or unexplained; breast imaging/biopsy for bloody or unilateral discharge.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.front: What is the first-line treatment for a prolactinoma?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.back: A dopamine agonist (cabergoline or bromocriptine), which lowers prolactin and shrinks the tumour, even for macroadenomas; surgery is reserved for resistant or compressive cases.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.front: Which non-endocrine renal condition causes hyperprolactinaemia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.back: Chronic kidney disease, through reduced prolactin clearance.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.front: Besides galactorrhoea, what symptoms commonly accompany hyperprolactinaemia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Galactorrhoea.back: Amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea and reduced libido/infertility in women, and reduced libido, erectile dysfunction and (sometimes) gynaecomastia in men.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.front: What is acanthosis nigricans and where does it occur?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.back: Velvety, hyperpigmented thickening of the skin in the flexures — typically the neck, axillae and groin. It is usually a marker of insulin resistance.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.front: What is the commonest cause of acanthosis nigricans?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.back: Insulin resistance — obesity, type 2 diabetes and the metabolic syndrome; also PCOS. It is symmetrical and insidious, often with skin tags.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.front: What features distinguish malignant acanthosis nigricans?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.back: Rapid onset, extensive involvement including mucous membranes and palms ('tripe palms'), in an older, often non-obese patient with weight loss. It is paraneoplastic.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.front: Which malignancy is most commonly associated with malignant acanthosis nigricans?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.back: Gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma, most often gastric cancer; urgent upper GI endoscopy and CT are used to find the primary.
Velvety, thickened, ridged palms resembling tripe, a paraneoplastic finding often occurring with malignant acanthosis nigricans and internal adenocarcinoma.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.front: Which endocrine conditions (besides diabetes/PCOS) cause acanthosis nigricans?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.back: Cushing's syndrome and acromegaly, both of which cause insulin resistance.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.front: Which drugs can cause acanthosis nigricans?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.back: Nicotinic acid, corticosteroids, the combined oral contraceptive, insulin and protease inhibitors; it may improve on stopping the drug.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.front: How does acanthosis nigricans relate to PCOS?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.back: It reflects the insulin resistance of PCOS and typically occurs with hirsutism, oligomenorrhoea and obesity; confirm PCOS with androgens and pelvic ultrasound.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.front: What investigations are appropriate for benign (metabolic) acanthosis nigricans?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.back: HbA1c or fasting glucose and lipids to assess insulin resistance/metabolic syndrome, plus androgens and pelvic ultrasound if PCOS is suspected.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.front: What is the management of benign acanthosis nigricans?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.back: Treat the underlying insulin resistance with weight loss and lifestyle measures, manage diabetes/PCOS, and stop culprit drugs; topical keratolytics/retinoids can improve appearance.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.front: What should trigger a search for malignancy in a patient with acanthosis nigricans?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.back: Rapid, extensive change with mucosal or palmar involvement (tripe palms), weight loss, and onset in an older, non-obese patient; investigate with upper GI endoscopy and CT.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.front: Can malignant acanthosis nigricans improve, and how?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acanthosis Nigricans.back: Yes — the skin change may regress with successful treatment of the underlying malignancy.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.front: What causes acromegalic features and what is the usual source?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.back: Excess growth hormone/IGF-1, almost always from a pituitary somatotroph adenoma. If it occurs before epiphyseal fusion it causes gigantism.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.front: List the classic acromegalic facial and peripheral features.
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.back: Coarse facial features, a prominent brow and jaw (prognathism), enlarging hands and feet (rings/shoes no longer fit), macroglossia and interdental spacing, a deep voice, oily sweaty skin and skin tags.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.front: Why are old photographs useful in acromegaly?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.back: Because the changes are insidious over years; comparing current appearance with old photographs highlights the gradual coarsening of features.
A raised IGF-1 is the screening test, confirmed by failure of GH to suppress during an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT); a pituitary MRI then localises the tumour.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.front: What is the leading cause of death in acromegaly?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.back: Cardiovascular disease — hypertension and cardiomyopathy leading to heart failure (also arrhythmia and accelerated vascular disease).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.front: Which cancer risk is increased in acromegaly, and how is it managed?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.back: Colorectal polyps and cancer; patients enter colonoscopy surveillance.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.front: Which metabolic and sleep complications occur in acromegaly?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.back: Type 2 diabetes/impaired glucose tolerance (GH is diabetogenic) and obstructive sleep apnoea (from soft-tissue and tongue enlargement).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.front: What are the mass-effect complications of the pituitary tumour in acromegaly?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.back: Bitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm compression), hypopituitarism (compression of the normal gland), and pituitary apoplexy (sudden headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.front: Which nerve entrapment is characteristic of acromegaly?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.back: Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, due to soft-tissue swelling compressing the median nerve.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.front: With which hormone is GH commonly co-secreted, and which syndrome may acromegaly be part of?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.back: Prolactin (causing galactorrhoea); acromegaly may occur as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.front: What is the first-line treatment for acromegaly, and what medical options exist?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.back: Trans-sphenoidal surgery is first-line for most tumours; medical options include somatostatin analogues (octreotide/lanreotide), a GH-receptor antagonist (pegvisomant) and dopamine agonists, with radiotherapy for residual disease.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.front: How is pseudoacromegaly distinguished from true acromegaly?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Acromegalic Features.back: Pseudoacromegaly (from severe insulin resistance) causes acromegaloid features but with a normal IGF-1 and normal GH dynamics.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.front: What are the classic features of the cushingoid habitus?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.back: Central obesity, a moon face, a buffalo hump and supraclavicular fat pads, purple striae, proximal myopathy, thin easily-bruised skin, plethora, hypertension and hyperglycaemia.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.front: What is the commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome overall?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.back: Exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoids — oral, inhaled, topical or injected. Always ask about steroid use first.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.front: What are the two steps of the endogenous Cushing's work-up?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.back: First confirm hypercortisolism (overnight dexamethasone suppression, late-night salivary cortisol, or 24-hour urinary free cortisol); then measure plasma ACTH to distinguish ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent causes.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.front: How does plasma ACTH separate the causes of endogenous Cushing's?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.back: A raised/inappropriately normal ACTH indicates an ACTH-dependent cause (pituitary Cushing's disease or ectopic ACTH); a suppressed ACTH indicates an ACTH-independent cause (an adrenal tumour).
An ACTH-secreting pituitary corticotroph adenoma — the commonest endogenous cause of Cushing's syndrome; it typically suppresses on high-dose (not low-dose) dexamethasone.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.front: Which features suggest ectopic ACTH secretion?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.back: Rapid onset, weight loss, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, pigmentation and marked myopathy, often in a smoker; it is usually caused by a small-cell lung cancer or a carcinoid.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.front: Why must long-term glucocorticoids never be stopped abruptly?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.back: Chronic steroids suppress the HPA axis; abrupt withdrawal leaves the adrenals unable to respond, risking an adrenal (Addisonian) crisis. Steroids must be tapered with sick-day rules.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.front: What are the major complications of cortisol excess?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.back: Hypertension, diabetes/impaired glucose tolerance, osteoporosis and fractures, immunosuppression/infection, venous thromboembolism, proximal myopathy, poor wound healing and mood disturbance.
A mild cortisol elevation with overlapping features seen in obesity, alcohol excess, depression or poorly-controlled diabetes; the biochemistry normalises as the underlying cause is treated.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.front: Which imaging is used once the biochemical source is established?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.back: Pituitary MRI (with inferior petrosal sinus sampling if needed) for ACTH-dependent pituitary disease, CT chest/body for ectopic ACTH, and adrenal CT for ACTH-independent adrenal tumours.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.front: How is endogenous Cushing's syndrome treated?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.back: Surgery is first-line (trans-sphenoidal for pituitary, adrenalectomy for adrenal, resection of an ectopic tumour), with medical cortisol-lowering therapy (metyrapone/ketoconazole) as adjunct/bridge, plus treatment of complications.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.front: Which adrenal cause of Cushing's may also cause virilisation, and why?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Cushingoid Habitus.back: An adrenal carcinoma, because it can co-secrete androgens along with cortisol.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.front: Why does Addison's disease cause hyperpigmentation?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.back: Low cortisol removes negative feedback, so the pituitary secretes excess ACTH (and its MSH-like fragment), which stimulates melanocytes and darkens the skin — especially the palmar creases, buccal mucosa, scars and pressure points.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.front: Which biochemical abnormalities accompany Addison's disease?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.back: Hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia (from mineralocorticoid deficiency), sometimes hypoglycaemia, with postural hypotension, fatigue and weight loss.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.front: What is an adrenal (Addisonian) crisis and how is it managed?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.back: Acute decompensated adrenal insufficiency with shock, vomiting, hypoglycaemia and collapse, often triggered by illness. Treat immediately with IV hydrocortisone (100 mg IV/IM stat) and IV fluids (0.9% saline) before awaiting confirmatory tests.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.front: What is the key confirmatory test for Addison's disease?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.back: A short Synacthen (ACTH stimulation) test, alongside a 9am cortisol and ACTH; adrenal autoantibodies help identify autoimmune aetiology.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.front: How does ectopic ACTH secretion cause hyperpigmentation, and what condition does it signal?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.back: A tumour secretes ACTH, driving pigmentation and cushingoid features with hypokalaemia and weight loss; it usually signals a malignancy such as small-cell lung cancer.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.front: How can you clinically distinguish Addison's from ectopic ACTH as a cause of pigmentation?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.back: Addison's has low cortisol with adrenal insufficiency features (hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia); ectopic ACTH has high cortisol with cushingoid features, hypokalaemia and rapid onset in a smoker.
Haemochromatosis — iron overload causing bronze/slate-grey skin, diabetes, hepatomegaly, arthralgia, cardiomyopathy and hypogonadism.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.front: How is haemochromatosis screened for and confirmed?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.back: Raised ferritin and transferrin saturation, confirmed with HFE genetic testing (and liver assessment).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.front: Which non-endocrine systemic diseases cause a generalised change in skin pigmentation?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.back: Chronic kidney disease (a sallow, grey uraemic tint) and chronic liver disease.
Amiodarone (slate-grey), minocycline, some chemotherapy agents, gold and antimalarials; the timing and distribution follow the drug.
Enlargement of an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour with marked hyperpigmentation, occurring after bilateral adrenalectomy removes cortisol feedback.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.front: What sick-day advice must patients on steroid replacement for Addison's receive?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Hyperpigmentation (Add.back: To increase (typically double) their glucocorticoid dose during illness, and to use emergency parenteral hydrocortisone if unable to take oral medication or if vomiting, to prevent an adrenal crisis.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.front: What is pretibial myxoedema and where does it occur?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.back: An infiltrative dermopathy of Graves' disease: raised, waxy, non-pitting, red-brown/violaceous plaques over the shins (and dorsum of the feet), often with a 'peau d'orange' texture.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.front: Despite its name, which thyroid state is pretibial myxoedema associated with?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.back: Hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease) — NOT hypothyroidism. This is a common exam trap.
Glycosaminoglycan (mucin) deposition in the dermis, driven by TSH-receptor antibodies (the same autoimmune process as Graves' orbitopathy).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.front: What is the extrathyroidal triad of Graves' disease?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.back: Pretibial myxoedema, Graves' orbitopathy (exophthalmos) and thyroid acropachy (clubbing with periosteal new bone).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.front: How is pretibial myxoedema distinguished from cellulitis?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.back: Pretibial myxoedema is non-tender, non-warm, non-spreading and afebrile, whereas cellulitis is warm, tender, spreading and often febrile and requires antibiotics.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.front: Which antibody confirms the underlying autoimmune disease in pretibial myxoedema?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.back: TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb), which are positive in Graves' disease.
Clinically; if needed, skin biopsy shows dermal mucin/glycosaminoglycan deposition. Confirm the associated Graves' disease with TFTs and TRAb.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.front: What lifestyle factor worsens the extrathyroidal manifestations of Graves' disease?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.back: Smoking, which worsens both thyroid eye disease and pretibial myxoedema; smoking cessation is advised.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.front: How is troublesome pretibial myxoedema treated?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.back: The lesion is often mild and self-limiting; troublesome plaques are treated with potent topical corticosteroids under occlusion (with compression), alongside treating the underlying Graves' disease.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.front: Which shin conditions can mimic pretibial myxoedema?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.back: Cellulitis, venous stasis dermatitis (with pitting oedema and varicosities), necrobiosis lipoidica (in diabetics) and lymphoedema.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.front: Why is finding pretibial myxoedema clinically important beyond the skin?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Pretibial Myxoedema.back: It flags autoimmune Graves' disease, prompting treatment of the thyrotoxicosis (which can cause atrial fibrillation or thyroid storm) and assessment of potentially sight-threatening eye disease.
Clubbing with periosteal new bone formation of the digits, a rare extrathyroidal manifestation of Graves' disease completing the triad with pretibial myxoedema and orbitopathy.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.front: What is necrobiosis lipoidica and how does it appear?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.back: A granulomatous dermatosis presenting as well-demarcated shin plaques with a yellow-brown, waxy, atrophic centre showing visible telangiectasia and a raised red-brown border.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.front: What systemic disease is necrobiosis lipoidica strongly associated with?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.back: Diabetes mellitus (hence the older name 'necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum'); the skin finding may precede the diagnosis of diabetes.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.front: Does necrobiosis lipoidica correlate with glycaemic control?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.back: No — it does not reliably track glycaemic control, and improving control does not necessarily resolve the lesions.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.front: What complications can arise within necrobiosis lipoidica plaques?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.back: Ulceration (often after minor trauma) with poor healing and secondary infection, and rarely squamous cell carcinoma in long-standing, non-healing lesions.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.front: When should a necrobiosis lipoidica plaque be biopsied?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.back: When there is a non-healing ulcer, a new nodule, or atypical change, to exclude a squamous cell carcinoma.
Clinically; if uncertain, skin biopsy shows palisading granulomas with necrobiosis (collagen degeneration). Screen for diabetes with HbA1c.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.front: How is necrobiosis lipoidica distinguished from granuloma annulare?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.back: Granuloma annulare forms skin-coloured annular rings (typically on the hands/feet) without atrophy or telangiectasia, whereas necrobiosis lipoidica is atrophic and yellow-brown with telangiectasia.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.front: How is necrobiosis lipoidica distinguished from pretibial myxoedema?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.back: Pretibial myxoedema is waxy, non-pitting and associated with Graves' disease (peau d'orange), whereas necrobiosis lipoidica is atrophic, yellow-brown and telangiectatic and associated with diabetes.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.front: What is the first-line treatment for active necrobiosis lipoidica plaques?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.back: Potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids (applied to the active border, avoiding the atrophic centre), alongside optimising diabetes and protecting the skin from trauma.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.front: Which investigations are appropriate when necrobiosis lipoidica is found in a patient not known to have diabetes?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.back: Screening for diabetes with HbA1c/fasting glucose, since the lesion may precede the diagnosis; assess for diabetic complications if diabetes is confirmed.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.front: Why is foot and skin care important in a diabetic with necrobiosis lipoidica?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.back: The fragile plaques ulcerate easily and heal poorly, and diabetics are prone to foot infection, so trauma protection and prompt treatment of ulceration/infection are important.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.front: Which gender and site are most commonly affected by necrobiosis lipoidica?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Necrobiosis Lipoidica.back: It is commoner in women and typically affects the shins (pretibial region), often bilaterally.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.front: What does tetany (with Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs) indicate?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.back: Neuromuscular hyperexcitability due to hypocalcaemia (or reduced ionised calcium from alkalosis) until proven otherwise.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.front: How is Chvostek's sign elicited and what is a positive result?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.back: Tapping over the facial nerve just anterior to the ear; a positive result is an ipsilateral twitch of the facial muscles.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.front: How is Trousseau's sign elicited and what is a positive result?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.back: Inflating a blood-pressure cuff above systolic pressure for a few minutes; a positive result is carpopedal spasm (flexed wrist and MCP joints with extended fingers).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.front: What are the dangerous features of severe hypocalcaemia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.back: Laryngospasm (stridor/airway compromise), seizures, and a prolonged QT interval with arrhythmia; treat with IV calcium gluconate and cardiac monitoring.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.front: What is the commonest cause of acute hypoparathyroidism causing tetany?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.back: Post-surgical hypoparathyroidism after thyroidectomy, parathyroidectomy or neck surgery; check calcium early after such operations.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.front: How does PTH help classify the cause of hypocalcaemia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.back: A low/inappropriately normal PTH indicates hypoparathyroidism; a raised PTH indicates vitamin D deficiency, chronic kidney disease or PTH resistance (pseudohypoparathyroidism).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.front: Why must magnesium be checked in refractory hypocalcaemia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.back: Hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion and action, so hypocalcaemia will not correct until magnesium is replaced.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.front: How can respiratory alkalosis cause tetany with a normal total calcium?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.back: Alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin, lowering the ionised (free) calcium while the total remains normal; treat the hyperventilation rather than giving calcium.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.front: How does acute pancreatitis cause hypocalcaemia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.back: Calcium is sequestered by saponification with released fatty acids (fat necrosis), lowering serum calcium.
Resistance to PTH, causing hypocalcaemia with a raised PTH; it may be associated with short stature and a round face (Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype).
A prolonged QT interval, which predisposes to arrhythmia.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.front: How is symptomatic hypocalcaemia managed acutely and then longer term?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Tetany (Chvostek's & T.back: Acutely with IV calcium gluconate (and magnesium if low); longer term with oral calcium and active vitamin D (e.g. alfacalcidol) for hypoparathyroidism, or vitamin D replacement for deficiency, treating the underlying cause.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.front: What is a bitemporal hemianopia and where is the lesion?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.back: Loss of both temporal visual fields due to compression of the optic chiasm, which carries the crossing nasal-retinal fibres.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.front: What is the commonest cause of a bitemporal hemianopia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.back: A pituitary macroadenoma compressing the chiasm from below; a bitemporal defect is a pituitary/parasellar mass until proven otherwise.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.front: Which quadrants are affected first by a pituitary adenoma versus a craniopharyngioma?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.back: An adenoma compresses from below and affects the superior temporal quadrants first; a craniopharyngioma compresses from above and affects the inferior quadrants first.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.front: What are the two endocrine priorities once a bitemporal hemianopia is found?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.back: Image the pituitary with MRI, and assess pituitary function (screen for a functioning adenoma and for hypopituitarism/diabetes insipidus).

Sudden haemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary adenoma causing severe headache, rapid visual loss, ophthalmoplegia and acute hypopituitarism; it needs IV hydrocortisone, resuscitation and urgent surgery.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.front: Which functioning adenomas can present with a bitemporal hemianopia, and their clues?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.back: Prolactinoma (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea), acromegaly (coarse features/large hands) and Cushing's disease (cushingoid features).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.front: How does a pituitary mass cause hypopituitarism?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.back: By compressing the normal gland, causing secondary deficiencies (hypothyroidism, hypoadrenalism, hypogonadism), and sometimes posterior involvement causing diabetes insipidus.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.front: Which investigations confirm and characterise a bitemporal hemianopia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.back: Formal perimetry (Goldmann/automated) to map the defect, and pituitary MRI; plus a full pituitary hormone panel (prolactin, IGF-1, 9am cortisol/Synacthen, TFTs, gonadotrophins) and assessment for diabetes insipidus.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.front: What is the first-line treatment for a prolactinoma causing chiasmal compression?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.back: A dopamine agonist (cabergoline/bromocriptine), which usually shrinks the tumour and can relieve the compression; surgery is reserved for resistant or acutely compressive cases.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.front: What is the general treatment for non-prolactinoma pituitary masses causing a bitemporal hemianopia?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.back: Trans-sphenoidal surgery (with radiotherapy for residual disease), alongside hormone replacement for any deficiencies and monitoring of the visual fields.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.front: How does a bitemporal hemianopia differ from a homonymous hemianopia in localisation?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.back: A bitemporal hemianopia localises to the optic chiasm; a homonymous hemianopia is retrochiasmal (optic tract, radiation or occipital cortex).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.front: Besides pituitary adenoma, name other causes of chiasmal compression.
signs__ENDOCRINE__Bitemporal Hemianopia.back: Craniopharyngioma, meningioma, internal carotid artery aneurysm, Rathke's cleft cyst, metastasis and glioma.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: The anterior pituitary is derived embryologically from:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: The adenohypophysis develops from Rathke's pouch (oral ectoderm); the neurohypophysis is a diencephalic downgrowth.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: On H&E a region of the pituitary looks like pale nervous tissue with scattered pink Herring bodies. This is the:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: The posterior pituitary resembles nervous tissue (axons + pituicytes) and contains Herring bodies (stored neurosecretion).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: Which cell/hormone pairing is correct for an anterior pituitary acidophil?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: Acidophils are somatotrophs (GH) and lactotrophs (prolactin); ACTH, TSH and FSH/LH come from basophils.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: Which anterior pituitary hormones are made by basophils (B-FLAT)?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: Basophils produce FSH, LH, ACTH and TSH (B-FLAT); acidophils make GH and prolactin.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: Prolactin secretion is unique because it is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: Prolactin is under tonic dopamine inhibition, so loss of hypothalamic input (stalk damage) raises prolactin.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: ADH and oxytocin released from the posterior pituitary are synthesised in the:
options: Supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: They are made in hypothalamic supraoptic (ADH) and paraventricular (oxytocin) neurons and transported to the posterior lobe.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: The hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system delivers hypothalamic hormones to the:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: The portal system (two capillary beds in series) carries hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting hormones to the anterior pituitary.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: A 30-year-old woman has galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea; MRI shows a pituitary microadenoma. The most likely tumour and first-line treatment are:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: Prolactinoma is the commonest pituitary adenoma and is usually treated medically with a dopamine agonist (e.g. cabergoline).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: A large non-functioning pituitary adenoma classically causes which visual defect?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: Upward extension compresses the optic chiasm, producing bitemporal hemianopia.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: Herring bodies are best described as:
options: Dilated axon terminals storing ADH/oxytocin in the posterior lobe
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: Herring bodies are axonal dilatations in the posterior pituitary that store neurosecretory granules.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: Failure to lactate with hypopituitarism after a complicated delivery with major haemorrhage suggests:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: Sheehan syndrome is postpartum infarction of the enlarged pituitary after obstetric haemorrhage, causing hypopituitarism and failure to lactate.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: A calcified suprasellar cystic tumour in a child, derived from Rathke's pouch remnants, is a:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: Craniopharyngioma arises from Rathke's pouch remnants and is a calcified suprasellar tumour of childhood (with 'motor-oil' cyst fluid).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: Which is the DEFINITIVE method to classify an anterior pituitary adenoma?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: Hormone immunohistochemistry definitively identifies the hormone(s) produced; H&E colour is only a rough guide.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: Excess ADH secretion produces:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: SIADH (too much ADH) causes water retention with concentrated urine and dilutional hyponatraemia; deficient ADH causes diabetes insipidus.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: Which hypothalamic hormone increases both TSH and prolactin?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: TRH stimulates TSH release and also stimulates prolactin (hence hypothyroidism can raise prolactin).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: The supporting glial cells of the posterior pituitary are called:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: Pituicytes are the glial supporting cells of the neurohypophysis.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: Sudden severe headache, visual loss and collapse in a patient with a known pituitary macroadenoma suggests:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: Pituitary apoplexy is acute haemorrhage/infarction of an adenoma causing sudden headache, visual loss and hypopituitarism.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: A GH-secreting adenoma arising before epiphyseal fusion causes:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: Excess GH before growth-plate closure causes gigantism; after fusion it causes acromegaly.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: In Sheehan syndrome the ANTERIOR pituitary is selectively infarcted because it:
options: Depends on the low-pressure hypophyseal portal venous system
Is supplied directly by the inferior hypophyseal artery
Has no blood supply of its own
Is supplied only by the internal carotid
Shares its blood supply with the pineal gland
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: The anterior lobe is fed by the low-pressure hypophyseal portal system (superior hypophyseal artery -> median eminence -> portal veins); postpartum haemorrhage causes it to fail, infarcting the pregnancy-enlarged gland. The posterior lobe, supplied directly by the inferior hypophyseal artery, is usually spared (so DI is uncommon).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.question: The best test to confirm acromegaly is:
options: Failure of GH to suppress during an oral glucose tolerance test
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (a.explanation: GH is pulsatile, so a random level is unreliable; acromegaly is confirmed by failure of GH to suppress after an oral glucose load (screen first with IGF-1).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: The homogeneous pink material filling thyroid follicles is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: Follicles are filled with colloid — a store of thyroglobulin, the scaffold on which thyroid hormone is made; it is PAS-positive.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: Thyroid follicular epithelium that is tall and columnar with scalloped colloid indicates:
options: An active (stimulated) gland, e.g. Graves disease
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: Tall follicular cells with scalloped (resorption-vacuole) colloid indicate a hyperactive gland such as Graves disease.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: Which enzyme performs organification of iodide and coupling on thyroglobulin?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: TPO oxidises/organifies iodide and couples iodotyrosines to form T3/T4; NIS only traps iodide into the cell.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: Antithyroid drugs such as carbimazole act mainly by inhibiting:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: Carbimazole/methimazole inhibit thyroid peroxidase, blocking organification and coupling (PTU also blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: Parafollicular (C) cells are derived from which embryological source and secrete:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: C cells are neural-crest derived and secrete calcitonin, which lowers serum calcium.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: A thyroid tumour with optically clear nuclei, nuclear grooves and psammoma bodies is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: Papillary carcinoma is defined by nuclear features (Orphan-Annie clearing, grooves, pseudoinclusions) and often psammoma bodies; it is the commonest thyroid cancer.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: Follicular carcinoma is distinguished from follicular adenoma by:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: The diagnosis of follicular carcinoma requires demonstration of capsular and/or vascular invasion; cytology alone cannot distinguish it from adenoma.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: A thyroid mass secretes calcitonin and shows an amyloid stroma; the patient has a RET mutation. The diagnosis is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: Medullary carcinoma is a C-cell tumour secreting calcitonin with amyloid stroma, associated with MEN 2 (RET).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: Diffuse lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centres and Hurthle-cell change causing hypothyroidism is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: Hashimoto (chronic lymphocytic) thyroiditis shows lymphoid follicles with germinal centres and Hurthle cells, with anti-TPO antibodies and hypothyroidism.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: The main hormone secreted by the thyroid and its more active peripheral form are:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: The thyroid secretes mostly T4 (a prohormone), which is deiodinated peripherally to the more active T3.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: A midline neck swelling that moves upward on tongue protrusion is a:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: A thyroglossal duct cyst (remnant of thyroid descent from the foramen caecum) is midline and moves up with tongue protrusion/swallowing.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: The Wolff-Chaikoff effect refers to:
options: Iodine triggering hyperthyroidism in a nodular gland
A large iodide load transiently inhibiting thyroid hormone synthesis
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: Wolff-Chaikoff: excess iodide transiently suppresses hormone synthesis; Jod-Basedow is iodine-induced hyperthyroidism in an autonomous gland.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: Which markers confirm follicular (thyroid epithelial) differentiation?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: Thyroglobulin and TTF-1 mark follicular cells and differentiated thyroid carcinomas; calcitonin/chromogranin mark C cells.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: Calcitonin from C cells lowers serum calcium by:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: Calcitonin inhibits osteoclasts, lowering serum calcium — the opposite of PTH (though minor in adult humans).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: TSH from the pituitary primarily acts on the thyroid to:
options: Stimulate follicular-cell growth and thyroid hormone synthesis/release
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: TSH drives follicular-cell hypertrophy/hyperplasia and thyroid hormone synthesis and release; chronic drive causes goitre.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: Papillary thyroid carcinoma most characteristically spreads via:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: Papillary carcinoma typically spreads via lymphatics to cervical nodes; follicular carcinoma spreads haematogenously.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: A painful thyroid after a viral illness with granulomas and multinucleate giant cells around follicles is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: De Quervain thyroiditis is a painful, often post-viral granulomatous thyroiditis with giant cells and transient hyperthyroidism.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: In which layer/location do C cells sit relative to the follicle?
options: Within the follicular basement membrane, not contacting colloid
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: C cells lie within the follicular basement membrane adjacent to follicular cells but do not reach the colloid.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: A child has goitre and sensorineural deafness from a defect in the apical iodide transporter. This is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: Pendred syndrome is an autosomal recessive defect of pendrin (the apical iodide/chloride transporter), causing dyshormonogenetic goitre with sensorineural deafness.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.question: Propylthiouracil is preferred over carbimazole in which situation, and why?
options: Long-term maintenance, because it is safer
Children, because it is a prodrug
The first trimester of pregnancy and thyroid storm, because it also blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion
histology__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland.explanation: PTU is preferred in the first trimester (carbimazole is more teratogenic) and in thyroid storm because, besides blocking TPO, it inhibits peripheral D1 deiodinase (T4->T3); carbimazole/methimazole are preferred otherwise (PTU carries hepatotoxicity risk).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: Which cell of the parathyroid gland secretes PTH?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: Chief (principal) cells secrete PTH; oxyphil cells have an uncertain role.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: Parathyroid tissue is most reliably distinguished from thyroid or lymph node on H&E by the presence of:
options: Intraglandular adipose tissue with cords of chief cells
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: Cords of chief (and oxyphil) cells in a background of fat identify parathyroid; thyroid has follicles/colloid and lymph node has germinal centres.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: Chief cells increase PTH secretion in response to:
options: Low serum calcium (sensed by the CaSR)
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: PTH secretion is inversely related to serum calcium, sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR): low Ca2+ drives PTH up.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: Which is a direct renal action of PTH?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: PTH decreases proximal phosphate reabsorption (phosphaturia), increases distal calcium reabsorption, and stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: The net biochemical effect of PTH is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: PTH raises serum calcium and lowers serum phosphate (renal phosphate wasting dominates).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: Larger, intensely eosinophilic parathyroid cells packed with mitochondria that appear at puberty are:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: Oxyphil cells are larger, eosinophilic (mitochondria-rich) parathyroid cells that appear from puberty; their function is unclear.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: A patient has hypercalcaemia, low phosphate and an elevated PTH from a single enlarged gland. The diagnosis is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: High Ca, low phosphate and high PTH from one gland indicate a parathyroid adenoma causing primary hyperparathyroidism.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease has low/normal calcium, high phosphate and markedly raised PTH with hyperplasia of all four glands. This is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: Chronic low calcium (CKD/vitamin D deficiency) drives compensatory four-gland hyperplasia with high PTH — secondary hyperparathyroidism.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: PTH increases bone resorption by acting on osteoblasts to express:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: PTH stimulates osteoblasts to express RANKL, which activates osteoclasts (PTH does not act directly on osteoclasts, which lack PTH receptors).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: Mild hypercalcaemia with inappropriately LOW urinary calcium and a family history suggests:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: FHH is a CaSR loss-of-function disorder causing mild hypercalcaemia with low urine calcium; it is benign and should not be treated surgically.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: Which pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: The inferior parathyroids arise from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch (with the thymus); the superior parathyroids arise from the 4th.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: Hypocalcaemia with tetany, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs after a total thyroidectomy indicates:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: Inadvertent parathyroid damage/removal during thyroidectomy causes hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcaemia and neuromuscular irritability.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: The 'brown tumours' and cystic bone lesions of osteitis fibrosa cystica are caused by:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: Sustained high PTH drives osteoclastic resorption with fibrosis, cysts and haemorrhagic 'brown tumours' (osteitis fibrosa cystica).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: Which hormone directly stimulates intestinal calcium absorption?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: PTH acts on the gut indirectly by increasing calcitriol (active vitamin D), which directly stimulates intestinal calcium absorption.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: PTH secretion is controlled mainly by:
options: Serum calcium via the calcium-sensing receptor
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: Unlike most endocrine glands, the parathyroid is regulated by serum calcium directly through the CaSR, not by a pituitary hormone.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: A parathyroid adenoma typically shows which histological change?
options: A predominance of chief cells with loss of intraglandular fat and a rim of compressed normal gland
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: A chief-cell adenoma is a hypercellular nodule with reduced fat and a compressed rim of normal parathyroid.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: Which combination of tumours occurs in MEN 2A, alongside parathyroid disease?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: MEN 2A comprises parathyroid hyperplasia/adenoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma; MEN 1 involves parathyroid, pituitary and pancreas.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: Calcitonin, in contrast to PTH, acts to:
options: Lower serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: Calcitonin lowers serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts — the opposite of PTH — though it is only a minor regulator in adult humans.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: A patient with squamous lung cancer has high calcium, low phosphate and a SUPPRESSED PTH. The mechanism is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: PTHrP mimics PTH (high Ca, low phosphate) but is not detected by the PTH assay, so measured PTH is suppressed - PTH-independent hypercalcaemia of malignancy. Primary hyperparathyroidism instead has a high or inappropriately normal PTH.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.question: Low calcium, high phosphate but a HIGH PTH, with short 4th/5th metacarpals, indicates:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands.explanation: Pseudohypoparathyroidism is end-organ resistance to PTH (GNAS/Gs-alpha defect, Albright hereditary osteodystrophy), so PTH is high yet calcium is low and phosphate high - unlike true hypoparathyroidism, where PTH is low.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: Which adrenal cortical zone secretes aldosterone and is NOT under ACTH control?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: The zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone under control of angiotensin II and potassium (not ACTH); it lacks 17-hydroxylase so cannot make cortisol/androgens.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: Pale, lipid-laden 'spongiocytes' arranged in straight cords, secreting cortisol, are found in the:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: The zona fasciculata is the widest zone, composed of pale lipid-rich spongiocytes secreting cortisol under ACTH control.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are best described as:
options: Modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons without axons
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: Chromaffin cells are neural-crest-derived modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons that lack axons and secrete catecholamines into the blood.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: The main catecholamine secreted by the adrenal medulla is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: About 80% of medullary catecholamine output is adrenaline, with ~20% noradrenaline.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: Adrenaline synthesis (via PNMT) in the medulla depends on:
options: Cortisol delivered by the cortical portal blood supply
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: PNMT (noradrenaline to adrenaline) requires cortisol, which reaches the medulla via cortical sinusoids draining inward — the cortical 'portal' supply.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: A patient has hypertension, hypokalaemia and suppressed renin with an adrenal cortical adenoma. The diagnosis is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: Aldosterone excess from a glomerulosa adenoma (Conn syndrome) causes hypertension with hypokalaemia and low renin.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: 21-hydroxylase deficiency (congenital adrenal hyperplasia) causes:
options: Low cortisol/aldosterone with excess androgens (salt-wasting and virilisation)
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: Blocking 21-hydroxylase reduces cortisol and aldosterone and shunts precursors to androgens, causing salt-wasting and virilisation, with compensatory adrenal hyperplasia.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: A child with abdominal mass, small round blue cells forming Homer-Wright rosettes and raised urinary catecholamine metabolites has:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: Neuroblastoma is a malignant neural-crest tumour of young children (often adrenal medulla) with small round blue cells, Homer-Wright rosettes and elevated catecholamine metabolites.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: Which markers confirm an adrenal medullary (chromaffin) tumour?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: Chromogranin and synaptophysin are neuroendocrine markers of chromaffin cells; inhibin/Melan-A/SF-1 mark the cortex.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: Episodic hypertension, headache, palpitations and sweating with a medullary tumour suggests:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: Phaeochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting medullary tumour producing episodic hypertension, headache, palpitations and sweating.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage causing acute adrenal crisis in meningococcal sepsis is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is acute adrenal haemorrhage/failure classically from meningococcaemia.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: Hyperpigmentation in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison) is due to:
options: Elevated ACTH/POMC (MSH) from loss of cortisol feedback
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: Low cortisol removes feedback, raising ACTH and its POMC-derived MSH, which stimulates melanocytes to cause hyperpigmentation.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: In secondary adrenal insufficiency (ACTH deficiency), which secretion is largely preserved?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: Aldosterone (zona glomerulosa) is largely preserved because it is controlled by the renin-angiotensin system and potassium, not ACTH.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: The single vein draining the right adrenal gland empties into the:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: The right adrenal (central) vein drains to the IVC; the left drains to the left renal vein.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: Which zone of the cortex is characteristically eosinophilic due to lipofuscin and secretes androgens?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: The zona reticularis is more eosinophilic (lipofuscin) and secretes androgens (DHEA) under ACTH control.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: The corticomedullary junction on a slide is marked by:
options: An abrupt change from pale lipid-rich cortical cells to more basophilic medullary cells
A change from basophilic to pale cells
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: The junction shows an abrupt transition from pale lipid-laden cortical cells to the basophilic chromaffin cells of the medulla.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: Cushing syndrome is characterised by excess of which hormone?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: Cushing syndrome results from cortisol excess, causing central obesity, striae, hypertension and glucose intolerance.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: Which statement about the adrenal medulla's innervation is correct?
options: It is innervated by postganglionic sympathetic axons
It is directly innervated by preganglionic sympathetic fibres releasing acetylcholine
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: The medulla behaves like a sympathetic ganglion: preganglionic sympathetic fibres synapse directly on chromaffin cells (using acetylcholine), which then release catecholamines.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: Before surgery for a phaeochromocytoma, blood pressure must be controlled with:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: Alpha-blockade must precede beta-blockade; giving a beta-blocker first leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, precipitating a hypertensive crisis. Diagnosis is by plasma/urinary metanephrines.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.question: In the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test, cortisol suppresses in which cause of Cushing's?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cor.explanation: High-dose dexamethasone suppresses cortisol from a pituitary source (Cushing disease), which retains some feedback sensitivity, but does not suppress ectopic ACTH or autonomous adrenal tumours.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: A pale, rounded cluster of cells with a rich capillary network, standing out among darker eosinophilic acini in the pancreas, is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: Islets of Langerhans appear as pale cell clusters among the darker exocrine acini; the acini secrete digestive enzymes into ducts.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: Which islet cell type is most numerous and what does it secrete?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: Beta cells (~70%, central) secrete insulin; alpha cells (~20%) secrete glucagon.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: In glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, the immediate effect of rising intracellular ATP is to:
options: Close K-ATP channels, depolarising the beta cell
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: Rising ATP closes the K-ATP channel, depolarising the membrane so that voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open and insulin is exocytosed.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: Sulfonylureas increase insulin secretion by:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: Sulfonylureas close the beta-cell K-ATP channel directly, forcing depolarisation and insulin release.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: Insulin-stimulated glucose uptake into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue uses which transporter?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: GLUT4 mediates insulin-dependent glucose uptake in muscle and fat; GLUT2 is the high-capacity glucose transporter of the beta cell and liver (glucokinase is the rate-limiting glucose sensor).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: Somatostatin from delta cells acts to:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: Somatostatin is a paracrine inhibitor of both insulin and glucagon (and of gut secretion/motility).

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: Autoimmune T-cell destruction of beta cells with lymphocytic 'insulitis' causes:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is due to autoimmune beta-cell destruction (insulitis), causing absolute insulin deficiency.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: Deposition of amyloid derived from IAPP within islets is characteristic of:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: Islet amyloid (from IAPP/amylin) accumulates in type 2 diabetes, alongside insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: A patient has fasting hypoglycaemia with symptoms relieved by glucose, and high insulin AND high C-peptide. The diagnosis is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: High insulin with high C-peptide indicates endogenous overproduction (insulinoma); exogenous insulin would suppress C-peptide.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: Refractory multiple peptic ulcers and diarrhoea due to a pancreatic islet tumour indicate a:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: A gastrinoma causes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with acid hypersecretion, multiple ulcers and diarrhoea.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: Necrolytic migratory erythema with weight loss and new diabetes suggests a:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: A glucagonoma (alpha-cell tumour) classically causes necrolytic migratory erythema, hyperglycaemia/diabetes and weight loss.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: Which markers confirm that a pancreatic tumour is neuroendocrine (islet-derived)?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: Chromogranin and synaptophysin are neuroendocrine markers; specific hormone immunostains subtype the tumour.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: C-peptide is clinically useful because it:
options: Is a component of injected insulin
Reflects endogenous insulin secretion (co-secreted with insulin)
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: C-peptide is cleaved from proinsulin and co-secreted with endogenous insulin, so it reflects the body's own insulin production.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: Blood from the islets drains next to the surrounding acini, so that insulin promotes exocrine function. This is the:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: The insulo-acinar portal system delivers islet-rich (insulin) blood to the exocrine acini, coupling endocrine and exocrine pancreas.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: Glucagon is released in response to:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: Alpha cells release glucagon during fasting/hypoglycaemia to raise glucose via glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: Which cell secretes ghrelin within the islet?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: Epsilon cells secrete ghrelin; beta=insulin, alpha=glucagon, delta=somatostatin, PP=pancreatic polypeptide.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: The glucose sensor transporter of the pancreatic beta cell is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: Beta cells take up glucose via GLUT2, allowing intracellular glucose to track blood glucose and set insulin secretion.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: Watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome) are caused by a:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: A VIPoma (vasoactive intestinal peptide tumour) causes the WDHA/Verner-Morrison syndrome of watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia and achlorhydria.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: The rate-limiting glucose sensor of the pancreatic beta cell is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: GLUT2 lets intracellular glucose equilibrate with blood, but glucokinase (high-Km hexokinase IV) is the rate-limiting step that makes ATP - and thus insulin secretion - track blood glucose. MODY2 is a glucokinase mutation.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.question: A non-obese teenager has mild stable hyperglycaemia, a strong autosomal-dominant family history, and no islet autoantibodies. The likely diagnosis is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets.explanation: MODY is autosomal-dominant diabetes of the young without autoantibodies or ketosis; glucokinase (MODY2) causes mild stable hyperglycaemia and HNF1A (MODY3) is sulfonylurea-sensitive.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: The pineal gland is located in the:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: The pineal lies in the epithalamus at the roof of the third ventricle, in the midline.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: The principal hormone of the pineal gland is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Pinealocytes secrete melatonin (made from serotonin), which entrains the circadian rhythm.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: Laminated calcified concretions characteristic of the pineal gland are called:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Corpora arenacea ('brain sand') are age-related calcifications diagnostic of the pineal and useful as a midline radiological landmark.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: Melatonin secretion is:
options: High at night/in darkness, low in daylight
High in daylight, low at night
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Melatonin follows a circadian rhythm with high levels in darkness and low levels in light.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: The pathway controlling the pineal runs from the retina to the pinealocytes via the:
options: Optic radiations to the occipital cortex
Suprachiasmatic nucleus and then the sympathetic superior cervical ganglion
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Light input reaches the SCN (master clock), which relays via sympathetic fibres through the superior cervical ganglion to the pineal.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: Melatonin is synthesised from:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Melatonin is made from serotonin (via N-acetylserotonin) in pinealocytes.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: Which immunostain marks pinealocytes?
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Pinealocytes are neuroendocrine and stain for synaptophysin and NSE; the interstitial glia are GFAP-positive.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: A child with a pineal region tumour develops paralysis of upward gaze. This is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Parinaud syndrome (dorsal midbrain syndrome) with upgaze palsy results from a pineal mass compressing the tectal plate.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: The commonest tumour of the pineal region is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Germinoma is the most common pineal region tumour; pineocytoma/pineoblastoma arise from pinealocytes.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: A pineal region mass can cause hydrocephalus by compressing the:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Compression of the cerebral aqueduct obstructs CSF flow, causing obstructive hydrocephalus and raised ICP.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: Effect of environmental light on melatonin:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Light inhibits the pineal pathway so melatonin is low by day; darkness increases sympathetic drive and melatonin.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: The interstitial cells of the pineal gland are best described as:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: The interstitial cells are astrocyte-like glia and stain for GFAP; the pinealocytes are the secretory neuroendocrine cells.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: Precocious puberty from a pineal region tumour may occur because of:
options: Compression of the pituitary stalk only
Loss of pineal antigonadotropic effect or an hCG-secreting germinoma
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Destruction of antigonadotropic pineal function or hCG secretion by a germinoma can cause precocious puberty.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: The pineal gland is often described as a neuroendocrine transducer because it:
options: Converts a neural (light) signal into a hormonal (melatonin) signal
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: It transduces environmental light-dark information (neural input) into the circulating hormone melatonin.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: Which clinical use of melatonin is well recognised?
options: Managing jet lag and circadian sleep disorders
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Melatonin is used for jet lag, shift-work sleep disturbance and other circadian rhythm sleep disorders.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: Pineal calcification on a skull radiograph or CT is useful because it:
options: Serves as a midline landmark whose shift suggests a mass
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Age-related pineal (corpora arenacea) calcification is a midline marker; displacement suggests a space-occupying lesion.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: The rate-limiting, light-suppressed enzyme of melatonin synthesis is:
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: AANAT (arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase) converts serotonin to N-acetylserotonin and is the rate-limiting, light-suppressed step; its activity rises in darkness, driving the nocturnal melatonin peak.

histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.question: Circadian light information reaches the suprachiasmatic nucleus from the retina via:
options: Rods and cones through the optic radiations
Melanopsin-containing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs)
histology__ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland.explanation: Melanopsin-expressing ipRGCs project via the retinohypothalamic tract to the SCN, providing non-image-forming light input that entrains the circadian clock - distinct from the rod/cone visual pathway.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.question: A 40-year-old woman has a diffuse, smooth goitre with a bruit, weight loss, tremor and exophthalmos. What is the diagnosis and confirmatory antibody?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.explanation: A diffuse toxic goitre with a bruit and eye signs is Graves' disease, confirmed by positive TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.question: A 55-year-old has a hard, fixed thyroid nodule that has grown quickly, with a hoarse voice and a firm cervical node. What is the priority investigation?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.explanation: A hard, fixed, rapidly growing nodule with hoarseness and lymphadenopathy is thyroid cancer until proven otherwise; ultrasound and FNA are the priority.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.question: A patient with a large goitre develops facial congestion and cyanosis on raising both arms. What does this sign indicate?
options: Retrosternal goitre causing thoracic-inlet obstruction (positive Pemberton's sign)
signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.explanation: A positive Pemberton's sign indicates a retrosternal goitre obstructing the thoracic inlet and SVC.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.question: A 60-year-old woman has a diffuse, firm, rubbery goitre, fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance. Which antibody is most likely positive?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.explanation: A firm goitre with hypothyroid features is Hashimoto's thyroiditis, associated with positive anti-TPO antibodies.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.question: A euthyroid patient has a long-standing goitre containing multiple nodules. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.explanation: Multiple nodules in a long-standing euthyroid goitre indicate a (non-toxic) multinodular goitre.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.question: A patient has a painful, tender goitre and thyrotoxic symptoms two weeks after a viral illness, with a raised ESR and low radioiodine uptake. What is the diagnosis?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.explanation: A painful post-viral goitre with a raised ESR and low uptake is subacute (De Quervain's) thyroiditis.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.question: A patient with a multinodular goitre becomes thyrotoxic. An uptake scan shows patchy hot areas. What is the diagnosis?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.explanation: Thyrotoxicosis from a multinodular goitre with patchy hot areas is toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer's disease).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.question: Which tumour marker is used to monitor medullary thyroid carcinoma?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma secretes calcitonin, which serves as a tumour marker; it may be part of MEN 2.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.question: What is the appropriate first-line investigation to characterise a solitary thyroid nodule?
options: Thyroid ultrasound (with FNA of suspicious nodules)
signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.explanation: Thyroid ultrasound characterises the nodule and guides FNA of suspicious features.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.question: A young pregnant woman has a diffuse, soft, non-tender goitre and is clinically and biochemically euthyroid. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassurance and monitoring once malignancy and compression are excluded
Immediate FNA of the whole gland
signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.explanation: A soft diffuse euthyroid goitre in pregnancy is usually physiological; reassurance and monitoring are appropriate after excluding malignancy and compression.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.question: Which feature would most strongly prompt cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) of a goitre?
options: Retrosternal extension with stridor or dysphagia
signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.explanation: Retrosternal extension with compressive symptoms warrants CT/MRI to define the extent (avoiding iodinated contrast if radioiodine is planned).

signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.question: A patient has a solitary autonomous 'hot' nodule on uptake scanning with suppressed TSH. What is the diagnosis?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Goitre.explanation: A single autonomous hot nodule causing thyrotoxicosis is a toxic adenoma; hot nodules are rarely malignant.

signs__ENDOCRINE__Bulging Eyes / Exophth.question: A 45-year-old woman has bilateral bulging eyes with lid retraction, lid lag and a fine tremor. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__ENDOCRINE__Bulging Eyes / Exophth.explanation: Bilateral proptosis with lid retraction, lid lag and thyrotoxic signs is thyroid eye disease (Graves' orbitopathy).
